name: Campanula Purple
lede: Campanula Purple is a greyish blue-violet named for the bellflowers, one of the 110 colors in the nomenclature Abraham Werner built for minerals and Patrick Syme adapted for naturalists.

sections.title: A mineralogist's purple
sections.body:
In Syme's Werner-based chart the color is number 39 in the purples, flanked by Pansy Purple and Imperial Purple [1][2]. The chart's examples are a vegetable one, the Canterbury bell, *Campanula persicifolia*, and a mineral one, the fluorite called fluor spar [1][2]. Each color in the chart is paired with an animal, a vegetable and a mineral example, so one name could be checked against living and mineral specimens [3].

Several neighboring purple names are renamed blues from older authors: Violet Purple was Werner's Violet Blue, Lavender Purple was Werner's Lavender Blue, and Plum Purple was the Plum Blue of Werner and Jameson, renamed when Syme added purple as a principal color [4].

sections.title: Where it was seen
sections.body:
The modern edition shows the color on a butterfly's wings, in the Camberwell Beauty of Duncan's *British Butterflies* of 1840 [2]. It also names the petals of the peach-leaved bellflower from Loudon's flower book of 1849, and the fluorite plate in Kurr's *The Mineral Kingdom* of 1859 [2]. A bellflower, a butterfly and a crystal share one patch of grey-violet.

The swatch here is an aged scan, approximate, and it matches ISCC-NBS block 245 [1]. The nearest everyday name on screen is [[slate]], ΔE 12.9 away [1]. Compared with [[purple]] or [[violet]], it is much greyer, closer to the shadow side of a [[periwinkle]].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
A color within six units of this swatch fills at least five per cent of the canvas in 37 of 23,781 archive paintings [5]. Henri Matisse carries it in 4 of his 50 works, a rate 51 times the archive's [5]. Munch has it in 3 of 50 [5]. Cézanne's [[painting:commons-Q64211180|Harlequin]] of 1888 holds it across 35 per cent, and Eugen's [[painting:smk-KMS3401|Ships at Anchor, Winter]] of 1908 across 29 per cent [5].

The match rate climbs in the 1900s, 15 hits among 1,674 paintings [5]. Norway has the highest lift of any country, at 16 times, from 3 of 120 paintings [5]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so this is a color match and not a pigment test [5]. The word *campanula* itself peaked in printed English in 1823 [6].

'Werner's own examples' changed to the chart's examples (they are Syme's).
